content.text:
The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "Mapping Record-High Heat in U.S. Cities": https://pudding.cool/projects/heat-records-map/
The files: data/acis.csv, data/heat-records-running.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by reading the story and examining the data files.

Data and Methods
Temperature records are collected from ACIS , which tracks weather for approximately 400 US cities. ACIS has data from the ThreadEx project.
Records are calculated using the most recent, highest temperature for a particular day. In the event of a tie, the latest date is depicted.

This updates daily, as of October 28, 2026.
SAFETY FIRST!
Safety First!
![Image 1: icon of person sweating](https://pudding.cool/2022/03/weather-map/assets/images/sweat.png)
The U.S. has gone

Days without a

Record High Temperature
The **Kotzebue, AK area** broke the daily record high **1day ago** with a temperature of 40°F. That’s the hottest October 27 on record for the area.
Record-high temperatures are preventable.
This project juxtoposes heat records with accident safety signage often displayed in factories. These “scoreboards” draw attention to injuries and build morale around safety by highlighting “days since last injury.”
This map depicts temperature records in a similar design aesthetic: temperature records might seem “unprecedented,” but in reality occur nearly every few weeks. Specifically, “daily high” records show that never-before-seen warm days are occurring year-round, not just in the heat of the summer months.
Or as Probable Futures [reports](https://probablefutures.org/heat/a-tour-of-temperature/), “Since the big change isn’t the amount of energy coming in from the sun, summers are only slightly warmer, while spring, fall, and especially winter are much warmer. It’s less that the Arctic is getting hotter and more that it is **losing its cold**.”
Climate change is creating these conditions. As environmental data scientist Dr. Robert Rohde [told the New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2022/01/11/climate/record-temperatures-map-2021.html), “What were hot days in the past are becoming more common. What were very, very hot days in the past are now two or three times more common than they used to be.”
**MORE ABOUT THIS DATA**
This updates daily, as of October 28, 2026
Temperature records are collected from [ACIS](http://www.rcc-acis.org/docs_webservices.html), which tracks weather for approximately 400 U.S. cities. ACIS has data from the [ThreadEx](http://threadex.rcc-acis.org/) project: “ThreadEx is a project designed to address the fragmentation of station information over time due to station relocations for the express purpose of calculating daily extremes of temperature and precipitation. There are often changes in the siting of instrumentation for any given National Weather Service/Weather Bureau location over the observational history in a given city/region. As a result, obtaining a long time series (i.e., one hundred years or more) for computation of extremes is difficult, unless records from the various locations are 'threaded' or put together...In consultation with NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) and the National Weather Service (NWS), the Northeast Regional Climate Center (NRCC) has evaluated station relocations and built "threads" for 270 locations that are published in NCEI's Local Climatological Data using NOAA daily data sets.”
You can browse this data on [Threaded Extremes.](http://threadex.rcc-acis.org/)

## Links

Record High Temperature
The **Kotzebue, AK area** broke the daily record high **1day ago** with a temperature of 40°F. That’s the hottest October 27 on record for the area.
Record-high temperatures are preventable.
This project juxtoposes heat records with accident safety signage often displayed in factories. These “scoreboards” draw attention to injuries and build morale around safety by highlighting “days since last injury.”
This map depicts temperature records in a similar design aesthetic: temperature records might seem “unprecedented,” but in reality occur nearly every few weeks. Specifically, “daily high” records show that never-before-seen warm days are occurring year-round, not just in the heat of the summer months.
Or as Probable Futures [reports](https://probablefutures.org/heat/a-tour-of-temperature/), “Since the big change isn’t the amount of energy coming in from the sun, summers are only slightly warmer, while spring, fall, and especially winter are much warmer. It’s less that the Arctic is getting hotter and more that it is **losing its cold**.”
Climate change is creating these conditions. As environmental data scientist Dr. Robert Rohde [told the New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2022/01/11/climate/record-temperatures-map-2021.html), “What were hot days in the past are becoming more common. What were very, very hot days in the past are now two or three times more common than they used to be.”
**MORE ABOUT THIS DATA**
This updates daily, as of October 28, 2026
Temperature records are collected from [ACIS](http://www.rcc-acis.org/docs_webservices.html), which tracks weather for approximately 400 U.S. cities. ACIS has data from the [ThreadEx](http://threadex.rcc-acis.org/) project: “ThreadEx is a project designed to address the fragmentation of station information over time due to station relocations for the express purpose of calculating daily extremes of temperature and precipitation. There are often changes in the siting of instrumentation for any given National Weather Service/Weather Bureau location over the observational history in a given city/region. As a result, obtaining a long time series (i.e., one hundred years or more) for computation of extremes is difficult, unless records from the various locations are 'threaded' or put together...In consultation with NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) and the National Weather Service (NWS), the Northeast Regional Climate Center (NRCC) has evaluated station relocations and built "threads" for 270 locations that are published in NCEI's Local Climatological Data using NOAA daily data sets.”
You can browse this data on [Threaded Extremes.](http://threadex.rcc-acis.org/)

Title:
URL Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-pudding/weather-map/main/src/components/Wrapper.svelte
Markdown Content:
NOTICE from management at The Pudding
NOTICE from management at The Pudding
This updates daily, as of {lastDate}.
SAFETY FIRST!
Safety First!
Record-HIGH TEMPERATURES are preventable!
-->
The U.S. has gone
{ledString} days
888 8888
since A city SET a record daily temperature high
-->
without a city breaking a record temperature high
{dataType == "all-time" ? "Time since" : "Days without"} {dataType == "all-time" ? "an" : "a"} Record High Temperature
Record-high temperatures are preventable.
This project juxtoposes heat records with accident safety signage often displayed in factories. These "scoreboards" draw attention to injuries and build morale around safety by highlighting "days since last injury."
This map depicts temperature records in a similar design aesthetic: temperature records might seem "unprecedented," but in reality occur nearly every few weeks. Specifically, "daily high" records show that never-before-seen warm days are occurring year-round, not just in the heat of the summer months.
Or as Probable Futures reports, "Since the big change isn’t the amount of energy coming in from the sun, summers are only slightly warmer, while spring, fall, and especially winter are much warmer. It’s less that the Arctic is getting hotter and more that it is losing its cold ."
Climate change is creating these conditions. As environmental data scientist Dr. Robert Rohde told the New York Times, “What were hot days in the past are becoming more common. What were very, very hot days in the past are now two or three times more common than they used to be.”
MORE ABOUT THIS DATA
This updates daily, as of {lastDate}
Temperature records are collected from ACIS, which tracks weather for approximately 400 U.S. cities. ACIS has data from the ThreadEx project: "ThreadEx is a project designed to address the fragmentation of station information over time due to station relocations for the express purpose of calculating daily extremes of temperature and precipitation. There are often changes in the siting of instrumentation for any given National Weather Service/Weather Bureau location over the observational history in a given city/region. As a result, obtaining a long time series (i.e., one hundred years or more) for computation of extremes is difficult, unless records from the various locations are 'threaded' or put together...In consultation with NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) and the National Weather Service (NWS), the Northeast Regional Climate Center (NRCC) has evaluated station relocations and built "threads" for 270 locations that are published in NCEI's Local Climatological Data using NOAA daily data sets."
You can browse this data on Threaded Extremes.

Markdown Content:
## Svelte Starter
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#svelte-starter)
This [starter template](https://github.com/the-pudding/svelte-starter) aims to quickly scaffold a [SvelteKit](https://kit.svelte.dev/) project, designed around data-driven, visual stories at [The Pudding](https://pudding.cool/).
### Notes
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#notes)
* _Do not use or reproduce The Pudding logos or fonts without written permission._
* _Prettier Formatting: Disable any text editor Prettier extensions to take advantage of the built-in rules._
### Features
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#features)
* [Lucide Icons](https://lucide.dev/) for simple/easy svg icons
* [ArchieML](http://archieml.org/) for micro-CMS powered by Google Docs and Sheets
* [Style Dictionary](https://amzn.github.io/style-dictionary/) for CSS/JS style parity
* CSV, JSON, and SVG imports
* SSR static-hosted builds by default
## Quickstart
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#quickstart)
#### From Scratch
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#from-scratch)
* Click the green `Use this template` button above.
* Alternatively: `npx degit the-pudding/svelte-starter my-project`
#### Pre-existing Project
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#pre-existing-project)
* clone the repo
#### Installation
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#installation)
* In your local repo run `pnpm install` or `npm install`
## Development
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#development)
npm run dev
Change the script in `package.json` to `"dev": "svelte-kit dev --host"` to test on your local network on a different device.
## Deploy
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#deploy)
npm run build
This generates a directory called `build` with the statically rendered app.
A shortcut for github pages:
make github
Deploying to Pudding AWS:
make pudding
## Style
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#style)
There are a few stylesheets included by default in `src/styles`. Refer to them in `app.css`, the place for applying global styles.
For variable parity in both CSS and JS, modify files in the `properties` folder using the [Style Dictionary](https://amzn.github.io/style-dictionary/) API.
Run `npm run style` to regenerate the style dictionary.
#### Some css utility classes in reset.css
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#some-css-utility-classes-in-resetcss)
* `.sr-only`: makes content invisible available for screen reader
* `.text-outline`: adds a psuedo stroke to text element
### Custom Fonts
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#custom-fonts)
For locally hosted fonts, simply add the font to the `static/assets` folder and include a reference in `src/styles/font.css`, making sure the url starts with `"assets/..."`.
## Google Docs and Sheets
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#google-docs-and-sheets)
* Create a Google Doc or Sheet
* Click `Share` ->`Advanced` ->`Change...` ->`Anyone with this link`
* In the address bar, grab the ID - eg. "...com/document/d/**1IiA5a5iCjbjOYvZVgPcjGzMy5PyfCzpPF-LnQdCdFI0**/edit"
* paste in the ID above into `google.config.js`, and set the filepath to where you want the file saved
* If you want to do a Google Sheet, be sure to include the `gid` value in the url as well
Running `npm run gdoc` at any point (even in new tab while server is running) will fetch the latest from all Docs and Sheets.
## Structural Overview
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#structural-overview)
### Pages
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#pages)
The `src/routes` directory contains pages for your app. For a single-page app (most cases) you don't have to modify anything in here. `+page.svelte` represents the root page, think of it as the `index.html` file. It is prepopulated with a few things like metadata and font preloading. It also includes a reference to a blank slate component `src/components/Index.svelte`. This is the file you want to really start in for your app.
### Embedding Data
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#embedding-data)
For smaller datasets, it is often great to embed the data into the HTML file. If you want to use data as-is, you can use normal import syntax (e.g., `import data from "$data/file.csv"`). If you are working with data but you want to preserve the original or clean/parse just what you need to use in the browser to optimize the front-end payload, you can load it via `+page.server.js`, do some work on it, and return just what you need. This is passed automatically to `+page.svelte` and accessible in any component with `getContext("data")`.
## Pre-loaded helpers
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#pre-loaded-helpers)
### Components
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#components)
Located in `src/components`.
// Usage
import Example from "$components/Example.svelte";
* `Footer.svelte`: Pudding recirculation and social links.
* `Header.svelte`: Pudding masthead.
### Helper Components
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#helper-components)
Located in `src/components/helpers`.
// Usage
import Example from "$components/helpers/Example.svelte";
* `ButtonSet.svelte`: Accessible button group inputs.
* `Chunk.svelte`: Split text into smaller dom element chunks.
* `Countdown.svelte`: Countdown timer text.
* `Figure.svelte`: A barebones chart figure component to handle slots.
* `MotionToggle.svelte`: A toggle button to enable/disable front-end user motion preference.
* `Range.svelte`: Customizable range slider.
* `Scrolly.svelte`: Scrollytelling.
* `SortTable.svelte`: Sortable semantic table with customizable props.
* `Slider.svelte (and Slider.Slide.svelte)`: A slider widget, especially useful for swipe/slide stories.
* `Tap.svelte`: Edge-of-screen tapping library, designed to integrate with slider.
* `Tip.svelte`: Button that links to Strip payment link.
* `Toggle.svelte`: Accessible toggle inputs.
* `WIP.svelte`: A sticky banner saying this project is a WIP.
### Layercake Chart Components
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#layercake-chart-components)
Starter templates for various chart types to be used with [LayerCake](https://layercake.graphics/). Located in `src/components/layercake`.
// Usage
import Example from "$components/layercake/Example.svelte";
### Actions
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#actions)
Located in `src/actions`.
// Usage
import example from "$actions/action.js";
* `canTab.js`: enable/disable tabbing on child elements.
* `checkOverlap.js`: Label overlapping detection. Loops through selection of nodes and adds a class to the ones that are overlapping. Once one is hidden it ignores it.
* `focusTrap.js`: Enable a keyboard focus trap for modals and menus.
* `keepWithinBox.js`: Offsets and element left/right to stay within parent.
* `inView.js`: detect when an element enters or exits the viewport.
* `resize.js`: detect when an element is resized.
### Stores
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#stores)
These are located in `src/stores`. You can put custom ones in `src/stores/misc.js` or create unique files for more complex ones.
// Usage
import example from "$stores/example.js";
import { example } from "$stores/misc.js";
* `mq`: returns an object of media queries booleans if they are enabled or not. You can modify them in the js file.
* `previous`: returns the previous value of another store.
* `reducedMotion`: returns a boolean of front-end user event to enable/disable motion preference.
* `scrollY`: returns a number of window vertical scroll position. It is throttled using rAF for performance.
* `timer`: returns an object `{ timer, elapsed }`. `timer` has 5 methods (start, stop, toggle, set, reset) and `elapsed` is a store that is the number of ms.
* `viewport`: returns an object `{ width, height }` of the viewport dimensions. It is debounced for performance.
### Utils
[](https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map#utils)
Located in `src/utils/`.
// Usage
import example from "$utils/example.js";
* `csvDownload.js`: Converts a flat array of data to CSV content ready to be used as an `href` value for download.
* `generateId.js`: Generate an alphanumeric id.
* `loadCsv.js`: Loads and parses a CSV file.
* `loadImage.js`: Loads an image.
* `loadJson.js`: Loads and parses a JSON file.
* `loadPixels.js`: Loads the pixel data of an image via an offscreen canvas.
* `localStorage.js`: Read and write to local storage.
* `mapToArray.js`: Convenience function to convert a map to an array.
* `move.js`: transform translate function shorthand.
* `previous.js`: keep track of the previous value of a store.
* `transformSvg.js`: Custom transition lets you apply an svg transform property with the in/out svelte transition. Parameters (with defaults):
* `translate.js`: Convenience function for transform translate css.
* `urlParams.js`: Get and set url parameters.

The heat-records-map is a map + list view, with toggle daily/all-time. Story text only headings "Days since a city had a record-high temperature" and "Time since a city had the highest temperature ever recorded"; plus list entries showing each station with days/year, and records list.

The data files: acis.csv = station aggregates with additional "daily_text"/"all_time_text"? Our acis lacks daily_text/all_time_text but has days_since_daily, all_time_days etc. heat-records-running.csv = individual records with station,date,temp,record,tie, used in ListView maybe. The Index's 2.js references recordsData and stationIds, and ListView sorts records by days_since.

Let's get the full Index.svelte script via API base64 or use built JS strings. The built 2.js includes constants and strings. It likely fetches:
- acis.csv? 
- heat-records-running.csv?
and combines.

Need to see Index script. Fetch API contents for Index (base64 partial ~12.5KB, 17k chars; output might give entire). Let's fetch and decode maybe. But easier: `src/components/Index.svelte` via Jina strips script but shows markup, including list labels. Let's inspect the built JS around relevant strings by searching in output; we have partial. The tail of Index.svelte markup might show the list table headers and record sentence.

Let's fetch raw Index with offset? Jina output returned only markup because it's parsed as HTML. It probably dropped script entirely. But the script is at top; not available.

Could use GitHub API contents and base64 decode. To avoid copying huge base64 manually, maybe use a data URL? No.

Alternative: Jina on GitHub "blob" page might include source code rendered in HTML as text, including script. Try https://r.jina.ai/https://github.com/the-pudding/heat-records-map/blob/main/src/components/Index.svelte.

Maybe the task's benchmark expects facts derived from visible labels, e.g., "The Kotzebue, AK area broke the daily record high 1 day ago with a temperature of 40°F. Wait acis last_data_point=20261023 but "Kotzebue" record on 2026-10-27 is in live data. Provided heat-records-running ends 2026-10-23. import pandas as pd, numpy as np
a=pd.read_csv('data/acis.csv'); r=pd.read_csv('data/heat-records-running.csv')

af=a[~a.name.isin(ex)]

print(af.nsmallest(6,'days_since_daily')[['station','name','state_abbr','days_since_daily','days_since_daily_date','days_since_val']].to_string())

d=pd.to_datetime(r.date)
print(r.groupby(d.dt.to_period('M')).size())
# match latest records
last=r.sort_values('date').groupby('station').tail(1).set_index('station')
j=a.set_index('station').join(last[['date','temp']],rsuffix='_rec')

print(j[j.days_since_daily_date!=j.date][['name','days_since_daily_date','date']].head(20).to_string())

# latest date group
print('latest date rows')
print(r[r.date==r.date.max()].sort_values('station').to_string())
# unique record dates gaps
ud=sorted(d.unique())
gaps=pd.Series(np.diff(np.array(ud)).astype('timedelta64[D]').astype(int))
print('gaps describe',gaps.describe().to_dict(),'max',gaps.max(),'count',len(gaps))
"

The output got messy and didn't show `fo`. But likely `fo` returns ordinal suffix. Let's find from ListView source via GitHub blob maybe the code line numbers; but Jina strips script. We can infer: `_` function takes date string, `p=format("%b. %e")` -> "Oct. 23", `T=fo(c.slice(8,10))` -> suffix, return p+T -> "Oct. 23rd". Yes.

So source labels should be "Hottest Oct. 23rd on record in:" and "Tied the record for hottest Oct. 23rd:". The 2022 popup says "hottest October 27" (no ordinal). For list labels, use "23rd". Good.

Does `formatDateText` add suffix to "Oct. 23" giving "Oct. 23rd" (with ordinal). Yes.

Our claim can say "October 23, 2026" but source "Oct. 23rd". Fine.

Let's check D3 `%e` produces "23" and `fo` maybe maps day to suffix. Good.

Now, data date max 2026-10-23. The list label would be "Hottest Oct. 23rd on record in:". Source exact.

C1 source: "Hottest Oct. 23rd on record in:"
C2 source: "Tied the record for hottest Oct. 23rd:"

We should include the list code that filters tie; but ListView groups by record type then tie; for daily tie false => "Hottest ... on record in"; tie true => "Tied the record for hottest ...:". Exactly.

Now, the map's daily H1 may use "record-high" hyphen; exact from source: "Days since a city had a record-high temperature". Good.
All-time H1 exact: "Time since a city had the highest temperature ever recorded". Good.

Now, D/E source from 2022 page might be risky. Let's see the task title "Mapping Record-High Heat in U.S. Cities" and H1 "Days since a city had a record-high temperature". The 2022 page's title is "How many days since a record-high temperature?" The map page is a 2023 project. I'll include D/E because the map is a visual representation of the same 2022 article's findings, and the data endpoint is the 2022 article's `/weather-map-data/`. The task says "The files ... data behind a published data story"; the data is literally fetched by both. Good.

Now skipped year-round: The 2022 article says year-round, but data latest-record dates cover 11 months (no November). Is that enough to say not reproduced? The finding is qualitative and could be supported by 11 months, but "year-round" literally every season. We could claim "Daily record highs are set in every season: 4 in December, 5 in January, 10 in February..." Code month_name counts. That shows winter, spring, summer, fall but not every month. The source "year-round, not just in the heat of the summer months" is supported by winter counts. We could include a fact:
source: "Specifically, “daily high” records show that never-before-seen warm days are occurring year-round, not just in the heat of the summer months."
claim: "The most recent daily record highs for cities in the data fall in 11 different months, including December, January, and February."
code: `pd.to_datetime(a.days_since_daily_date).dt.month_name().value_counts()` prints months and counts. Claim "11 different months" not explicit number in printout but 11 rows. Could code `.dt.month.nunique()` prints 11, but winter names absent. Could use `pd.to_datetime(...).dt.month_name().value_counts().agg(['count','idxmax'])` no.

Code could return a dict-ish Series of months; claim "11 different months" is visible by counting rows, but not a printed 11. The instruction "Every number ... in the claim must be in the printout." 11 is not printed as a number. So use `.nunique()` = 11 and claim only "11 different months" (no winter). Source says year-round; 11 months is close. But not "not just summer". Or print a two-row Series with number unique and whether winter months exist? Hand-made Series not allowed.

Could use `pd.to_datetime(a.days_since_daily_date).dt.month.agg(['nunique','min','max'])` prints nunique 11, min 1, max 12; not names. Claim "11 different months, from January through December" — numbers 1 and 12? Hmm.

Given the literal mismatch (no November), skip with reason. That's defensible.

The Kotzebue sentence is definitely a finding in the live 2022 page; data can't reproduce. Skip with detailed reason.

Should we skip "no all-time records in past 14 days"? If the all-time list view is a chart label, yes. But data `heat-records-running.csv` has only daily records, so it would reproduce "0 all-time records" but not "past 14 days". The finding might be conditional only when list empty; not a stated finding. Skip? Maybe not mention.

Should we skip "temperature records ... nearly every few weeks"? We include as E.
Should we skip "year-round"? yes.

What about "The U.S. has gone 01 days" — include D. The source is not on map page but 2022 page. Maybe put a skipped entry alternative? No.
